title: ROAD: Retrospective Analysis of Ocrelizumab Use in Older Adults: A Real-World Data Analysis
summary:
Immunosenescence and MS Therapy in Advanced Age
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is traditionally defined as a disease of young adulthood. However, due to demographic shifts and significant advances in pharmacotherapy, the number of patients reaching their sixth decade of life with MS is steadily increasing. This patient group presents unique medical challenges, as the immune system undergoes a natural aging process known as immunosenescence. During this process, inflammatory mechanisms shift: while acute defensive capabilities decline, chronic, systemic inflammatory processes may become more prominent.

The Therapeutic Gap in Patients Over 55
Although highly effective therapies, such as the CD20 antibody Ocrelizumab, have revolutionized the standard of care, most data regarding their efficacy and safety originate from clinical pivotal trials involving younger participants. Consequently, an evidence gap exists for the 55+ age group. It is known that older patients may react physiologically differently to immunotherapy; at the same time, current data suggest that abruptly discontinuing treatment or switching to lower-efficacy preparations carries the risk of a resurgence in disease activity. Therefore, a precise risk-benefit assessment is essential during this stage of life.

The ROAD Study Concept: Insights from Real-World Clinical Practice
This is where the ROAD study comes in. Its objective is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Ocrelizumab in MS patients over the age of 55 under real-world conditions. Unlike controlled clinical trials, the ROAD study utilizes Real-World Data (RWD). This involves a retrospective analysis of routine clinical data sourced directly from patient records at a specialized medical center in Germany (a monocentric approach). This retrospective view allows for the analysis of treatment courses lasting up to seven years, provided patients have been receiving the medication for at least two years. To protect patient privacy, all parameters—such as laboratory values and radiological findings—are fully anonymized prior to analysis.

Central Analytical Parameters of the Investigation
The study focuses on several clinical pillars to evaluate disease control in older age. A primary aspect is clinical stability, measured by the annualized relapse rate. Parallel to this, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) serves as an objective benchmark for inflammatory quiescence within the central nervous system; specifically, the scans are monitored for new or active brain lesions.

Since Ocrelizumab specifically modulates the immune system, another focus lies on the immune status. Regular blood analyses monitor changes in the concentration of vital antibodies (immunoglobulins) and determine whether substitution therapy is required. The investigation is completed by a detailed documentation of the safety profile, with a particular emphasis on infection rates, comorbidities, and potential interactions with other medications commonly taken in older age.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•	Patients aged 55 years or older at the start of ocrelizumab treatment.
•	Start of OCR start only after 01.02.2018
•	Documented diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RMS) in the  patient’s medical records.
•	Availability of informed consent.
•	At least two years of documented ocrelizumab treatment in the patient’s medical history.
Exclusion criteria:
•	Patients younger than 55 years at the start of ocrelizumab treatment.
•	Documented diagnosis of primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS)
•	Lack of informed consent for data use
